name: the chat
statement: Members move the room's planning into a chat, an existing server or a new one, and invite helpers to it. They bring the chat's designs, decisions and warnings back to the thread. They argue which chat to use, whether a chat is needed or secure, whether it is official, and whether it may decide for the work or bind placers.
range: from one member posting the chat's link to a room whose design, borders and diplomacy are settled in the chat and reported in the thread
why: No element states the chat. P04 circulates a template, P17 states chats shared between rooms, and C01 names decided order; none states a room moving its own planning into a chat and bringing its decisions back (G59a). The propose lines show it in their own rooms (T3-014 holds most of them), and members also dispute which chat to use, its need, its security, its standing and its authority over placers (G59's readings 2, 3 and 12).

name: asking and explaining
statement: Members ask what the canvas is, how to place, what a call or a name means and what a picture shows, and others explain the rule, the timer, the controls, whose mark a picture is and what happened. They ask before, during and after the close, and some questions get no answer.
range: from one question about what the canvas is, left unanswered, to a thread that explains the five-minute rule, identifies the neighbouring pictures and tells what happened to the work
why: No element states members asking and explaining what the canvas and its pictures mean (G59a). The propose lines show it in their own rooms (T3-016 and T3-018 hold most of them): questions about the rule, the timer, the controls, calls, names and pictures, with answers or none, before, during and after the close (G59's readings 4, 5, 7, 10 and 14).

name: the work bringing people in
statement: The room's work brings people into the room. A viewer finds the sub through the mark or through a sign written to that end, a member of an ally comes through joint work, and a lapsed member returns. Members welcome them, explain the room's subject, take them into its usual activity, count the new subscribers and argue how to receive them.
range: from one visitor who says the logo brought them to a room that counts hundreds of new subscribers, welcomes them with guides and argues whether the influx spoils it
why: No element states the route from the mark back into the room; P01 states the opposite route, the room calling members out to the canvas (G59a). The propose lines show it in their own rooms (T3-044 holds most of them): viewers, members of allies and lapsed members brought in by the mark or a sign, and members welcoming, orienting and counting them and arguing how to receive them (G59's readings 1 to 3, 9 and 10). D3a-54 found 27 of 39 such returns before hour 73.

name: new jokes made of the work
statement: Members make new jokes out of the canvas work, its mistakes, its damage and its neighbours: puns on the mark, mock names and titles for a figure, and jokes about attackers and bots. The room takes the jokes up, and some members want a joke kept in the work.
range: from one pun on what the logo looks like to a running gag the room wants kept as flair
why: K04 states jokes and lore carried in from before the canvas; no element states new jokes made of the work (G59a). The propose lines show them in their own rooms (T3-031 holds most of them), and the room takes them up (G59's readings 8, 9 and 11).

name: choosing the spot
statement: Before any loss, the room chooses where to put its work and changes the spot while it builds. It looks for open room, weighs a crowded or contested place, shrinks or moves the design ahead of a neighbour or the void, restarts a misplaced start, and refuses to move once enough pixels are in.
range: from one member suggesting more space on the right to a room that drops two places and reshapes its design before it builds
why: P10 states moving only after the work is erased or overrun; no element states choosing and changing the spot before any loss (G59a). The propose lines show it in their own rooms (T3-020 and T3-022 hold most of them) (G59's reading 8).

name: a room formed for the canvas
statement: A room forms for the canvas around a mark. Members open a sub or a chat for a pattern or a figure and set it up. They invite the people seen building or copying the mark, give it a meaning its followers share, gather its repeaters into a group that can negotiate, and move or split the room.
range: from strangers copying a pattern before anyone speaks for it to a faction that opens a sub, names itself and moves its home
why: The model's rooms are host subs and their kindred groups, and K04 states a body carried in from before the canvas; no element states a room that the canvas made (G59a). The propose lines show members opening and setting up a sub or chat for a pattern or figure, inviting those seen building or copying it, naming it, gathering its repeaters to negotiate, and moving or splitting it (G59's readings 1, 8 and 11 to 14).

name: arguing offence
statement: Members argue whether a joke, a taunt or a word in canvas talk offends, and they refuse slurs and hate symbols. They object, correct, apologise, remove the words or tell the speaker to leave, and they cover swastikas or refuse to draw them.
range: from one member telling an attack caller to leave over slurs to a thread-long argument over a celebration's joke
why: P02 holds a swastika removed from the room's own mark; no element states the argument over offensive canvas talk or the refusal of slurs and hate symbols (G59a). The propose lines show it in their own rooms (T3-143 and T3-182 hold most of them) (G59's readings 13 and 14).

name: turning the work toward the people it shows
statement: The room turns its work toward people outside the canvas whom the mark shows or addresses: the creators, the team, the streamer, a company or the press. It shows them the work, hopes for their notice, shares the coverage and celebrates their acknowledgement, or it keeps the work from troubling them.
range: from one member asking to show the work to the group's staff to a room that celebrates the team sharing its screenshot
why: P11 states marking the finished work in the room and in the canvas sub; no element states turning the work toward the people it shows or addresses (G59a). The propose lines show members seeking, sharing and celebrating their notice, or sparing them trouble (G59's readings 13 and 14).

name: arguing whether covering is fair
statement: Members argue whether covering others' work is fair. Some call it betrayal, dirty or a cost to the room's name. Others answer that change is the canvas's point, that wiping makes room for new art, or that the canvas is a game of conquest. The argument runs during the work and after the close.
range: from one exchange over why people keep changing a figure to a room that argues after the close whether its canvas was conquest or drawing together
why: A16 states a refusal of an attack call with a reason that names the room's norm or the attack's cost; no element states the argument that runs both ways, without a call, during the work and after the close (G59a). The propose lines show it in their own rooms (G59's readings 10, 12 and 13).

name: stepping away under strain
statement: A member steps away from the work under strain, or the room repairs a quarrel between members. The work turns stressful or personal, or a member is criticised or yelled at over a pixel or a proposal. Others rebuke the harsh speaker, the speaker apologises, or the member threatens to leave or leaves.
range: from one member quitting because the canvas was stressful to a member yelled at over one wrong pixel who receives an apology
why: K02 states giving up when the room judges its hands or room too few; no element states a member stepping away under strain or a quarrel between members repaired (G59a). The propose lines show it in six rooms; three rows first ruled one room's were moved here when the rooms became six (G59's reading 13).

name: hiding plans from rivals
statement: Rooms keep their plans from rivals who read their threads, and they reach into rivals' venues. Members switch to their own language or write in code, move the plan to private messages, plant members in a rival's chat and warn of a snitch in their own.
range: from one call to speak Hindi because rivals read the strategy to members who admit they infiltrated a rival's voice chat
why: No element states concealment from rivals or reaching into their venues; P18 states the contest carried in talk and P09 the moves on the canvas (G59a). The propose lines show it in their own rooms (G59's reading 12).

name: turning on the room's own mark
statement: Members who object to the canvas posts in the sub turn against the room's own mark. One member says the posts make them tear down the logo, and one recruits trolls to ruin the flag.
range: two rooms only: one member's report of tearing down the logo, and one call to ruin the room's own flag; thin
why: P20 states members objecting to the canvas posts and arguing the canvas's worth; it does not state members damaging the room's own mark for that reason (G59a). Two rooms show the act, each in explicit words (G59's reading 11); it is kept as a candidate, named thin in its range.

name: members' own time and means
statement: Members place on their own time and with their own devices. They fit placing around sleep, study, exams, work and travel. They cannot place from a phone or while away, they leave when the wait is too long, they save pixels under the timer, they find the work addictive, and they report what it cost them.
range: from one member leaving the design overnight to sleep for classes to members who stayed up eight hours to repair
why: No element states the members' own time and means as a condition of the work (G59a). The propose lines show placing fitted around sleep, study, exams, work and travel, lost from phones, cut short by the wait, and its cost reported, in their own rooms (G59's readings 1, 6 to 8, 11, 12 and 14).

name: the site's limits and faults
statement: The site sets what members can do, and members report its faults and pass on fixes. They report a blank or stale canvas, the site down, a vanished or faulty timer, glitches that seem to give extra pixels, captchas, the official app required and the site blocked in a country. They refresh, update, keep a separate window and test whether extra pixels reach the canvas.
range: from one report that the canvas appears blank to members testing a glitch until they accept that its pixels show only in their own client
why: No element states the site as a condition; P14 states members adding machine hands, not the site's own faults and limits (G59a). The propose lines show faults reported and fixes passed on in their own rooms (G59's readings 11, 12 and 14).

name: members of both rooms
statement: Some members belong to both rooms in a contest or at a border. They say they are torn or proud of both, and the room reassures them or still counts them as its own.
range: from one member torn between two fandoms' works to a room teasing members who worked on another project as traitors who are still members; four rooms, thin
why: No element states members who belong to both sides; the model takes a room as the actor where its members speak or act for it, and these members say they act for neither or for both (G59a). Four rooms show it (G59's reading 13); named thin in its range.
